title: Elon Musk Says Money May Become 'Irrelevant,' His Fortune Could Vanish
summary:
Elon Musk says money could be meaningless one day, and the vast majority of his wealth will likely be gone within a few generations.
The world's richest person predicted that advances in robotics and space travel will create a multiplanetary economy, at which point "money becomes irrelevant" and "conventional currency will not matter."
The Tesla and SpaceX CEO shared his vision of a post-money future and his outlook on his personal fortune with his biographer, Walter Isaacson, on "The Builders" podcast.
He also outlined what he hopes his foundation will spend his fortune on after he's gone: "Continue the goals.
"If money won't matter in 2036, why don't you pledge to donate your current wealth of approximately $1 trillion to charity no later than 2036," Acemoglu wrote on X.

title: JustWatch now streams TV shows and movies, too
summary:
After announcing plans to introduce its own streaming service last month, JustWatch, a popular guide and search engine for finding things to watch on existing platforms like Disney Plus and Netflix, launched JustWatch TV today.
JustWatch TV Free includes a “curated selection of titles” available with ads, while the paid JustWatch TV Plus subscription has over 300 ad-free titles plus other exclusive app features like the ability to hide shows you’ve disliked or already watched in its guide.
The JustWatch TV Store will include a “growing selection of recent and popular movies to rent” but is initially only available in the US, UK, Ireland, Australia, and New Zealand.
JustWatch TV Plus will be priced at $3.99 per month and include a 10 percent discount on rentals, but the company is also offering a $49.99 lifetime subscription for a limited time.
Update, October 20th: Noted that the lifetime subscription is a limited-time offer.

title: Elon Musk says 'AI and robots' are the only way to solve America's debt burden
summary:
Elon Musk said artificial intelligence and robots — not government spending cuts — are the only way to fix the US national debt problem.
"I came to the conclusion that the only way we're going to solve the national debt is with AI and robots.
We're not going to solve it by trying to save our way there," Musk told Isaacson, calling the latter "impossible."
The US national debt load hit a record $40 trillion in August and has continued to climb, according to Treasury data.
"There will still be currency, but I think currency will be measured in fundamental physics metrics like wattage and tonnage, mass and energy," he said, predicting, "Conventional currency will not matter."

title: Jensen Huang has a message for Europe: stop overthinking AI or get left behind
summary:
That's the pointed message Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has delivered to European leaders during his trip to the continent over the past week.
Asked how Europe should regulate AI, Huang said safety had to be paramount, but cautioned that policymakers could not regulate their way to technological leadership.
"There's nothing to regulate if the industry doesn't thrive," Huang told Merz, arguing that Germany needed to foster a domestic AI industry while ensuring it developed safely and responsibly.
It was the same urgent message Huang had delivered in London days earlier.
If the continent spends too long debating how to regulate AI, it may find that the meaningful innovation is done elsewhere.

title: AMD is bringing FSR 4.1 to Xbox consoles and handhelds
summary:
AMD has just revealed that it’s bringing its latest upscaling technology, FSR 4.1, to the Xbox Series S and X consoles, as well as laptops, 6000-series GPUs, and both the Xbox Ally and Xbox Ally X handhelds.
And it’s coming fast — FSR 4.1 will start appearing for Radeon RX 6000-series GPUs today, as well as Ryzen AI Max 300 and 400 series devices and Ryzen AI 9 300 and 400 series devices.
FSR 4.1 can improve performance in more than 300 supported games, including Cyberpunk 2077, Battlefield 6, and Assassin’s Creed Shadows.
FSR 4.1 arrives just weeks after Sony and AMD teamed up to bring Quick Spectral Super Resolution (QSSR) to the base PS5, based on Sony and AMD’s Project Amethyst work.
Valve has not yet confirmed it will come to the Steam Deck, but it would be surprising if it didn’t: the Xbox Ally’s Z2 A chip, which is now getting FSR 4.1, is very similar to the one in the Deck.

title: UK working to identify exposure after global cyber-security warning
summary:
The UK government says it is working to identify any potential exposure in its online services, after critical cyber-security flaws were identified in the PHP programming language that underpins a significant number of the world's websites.
Governments and some of the world's biggest companies are rushing to protect systems that use PHP before hackers can exploit the flaws.
The flaws were first discovered by AI, after which governments urged anyone who uses PHP to address them.
A UK government spokesperson urged "all organisations, private and public, large and small" to follow guidance to protect their systems.
When you visit a website like Wikipedia, PHP is the code that collects information you need and presents it in a way you can read on the web.

title: Nvidia’s latest GPU driver brings a new way to speed up PC games
summary:
Nvidia is rolling out a new GPU driver today (621.01) that enables Microsoft’s new Advanced Shader Delivery technology to speed up game launches.
The technology also removes mid-game “just-in-time” shader compilation, reducing stuttering and CPU spikes.
Microsoft’s Advanced Shader Delivery works by offloading shader compilation for different hardware combinations to the cloud.
“This system is storefront-agnostic, meaning you benefit even when playing games purchased on Steam, as long as the Xbox PC app is installed on your PC,” says Burnes.
You can download Nvidia’s latest 621.01 update here, and Advanced Shader Delivery is also supported on AMD GPUs with Adrenalin 26.6.1 or higher and Qualcomm’s Snapdragon X2 series with driver version 2026.08.3 or higher.

title: A critical PHP vulnerability may take websites down today
summary:
Security patches for the PHP programming language, widely used to build websites and web apps, have rolled out today, with the goal of fixing two critical vulnerabilities that could wreak havoc on the internet if left unchecked.
In an advisory published on Tuesday, PHP developers said the vulnerabilities have a severity rating of 9.2 out of a possible 10, with some cybersecurity agencies encouraging websites to temporarily take their systems offline if they’re unable to apply the fix immediately.
The impact of these vulnerabilities could be vast, with one security researcher estimating that more than 1.3 million internet-connected hosts are likely affected.
Wordfence also warned that the fix can’t be installed using automatic updates, so site owners need to find out who is responsible for updating PHP to apply the patch manually.
Update, October 21st: Updated language to reflect that the security patches have now been released.

title: PHP: The three letters that shut down sites all over the internet today
summary:
The internet security site VirusTotal says its scanner currently registers about 3.8 million sites running PHP with at least one port open.
According to OpenAI, an AI security group called Calif identified a “critical” PHP flaw using GPT-5.6 Sol, and Google-owned Wiz independently discovered and reported the vulnerabilities using AI.
The PHP Group says that basically any site running PHP is at risk.
GoDaddy says that any site using PHP should assume it is affected and update to the fixed release as soon as possible.
It also says that sites running PHP 8.1 or older should upgrade to a newer version, as they’re no longer supported and there will not be an official fix coming.

title: Walmart is inviting AI agents to shop for you
summary:
Walmart will soon let AI agents shop on its website for you.
The embrace of AI agents stands in stark contrast to Amazon, which blocked Perplexity’s shopping agent and Meta’s Muse AI assistant.
By default, Walmart will require approval for all AI agent purchases, but you can also let it shop within a certain budget, such as up to $100.
The retailer has built an “Agent Gateway,” currently available in beta, that connects AI agents through the Model Context Protocol, an open standard that allows AI agents to plug into different services on the web.
The company will let users shop with AI agents on Sam’s Club as well.

title: Spotify pulled 50 million AI slop and spam tracks from its recommendations
summary:
Is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more.
Spotify says it has removed more than 50 million songs considered AI-generated slop or spam from user recommendations over the past year.
“Our editors hold the same standard and don’t program content identified as slop or spam,” Spotify says.
Last year, the company said it took down more than 75 million songs identified as spam.
It’s also partnering with Universal Music Group and the independent music publisher Believe to launch a tool for creating AI music remixes.

title: Infrastructure startup Fireworks AI is in early talks for new funding at a valuation between $30 billion and $40 billion
summary:
Fireworks AI is seeking to raise fresh funding at a valuation between $30 billion and $40 billion, a dramatic jump just months after the AI-infrastructure startup was valued at $17.5 billion, according to people familiar with the matter.
The potential valuation leap reflects investors' appetite for the companies selling the computing power and tools fueling the AI boom, even as Fireworks AI works through the fallout from a recent security incident.
The company rents out computing infrastructure and software that lets businesses run, fine-tune, and deploy open-weight and custom AI models.
That round followed a $250 million Series C at a $4 billion valuation in late 2025, co-led by Lightspeed, Index, and Evantic.
The fundraising talks come shortly after a security incident at Fireworks AI.

title: Jackdaw: Will it cut energy bills and how much gas will it provide?
summary:
However, NSTA estimates that Norwegian North Sea gas production - which Britain already imports by pipeline in large volumes - has a considerably lower average emissions impact than that of the UK's existing North Sea gas production.
This is because UK North Sea gas mostly comes from smaller fields and is extracted with older infrastructure and technology than those of Norway.
So the impact on the environment of the Jackdaw decision partly depends on what happens to the mix of UK gas consumption in future - and where it comes from - which is uncertain.
If additional gas production from Jackdaw displaces US LNG imports, UK-related national emissions could be lower than otherwise.
But if additional gas production from Jackdaw displaces gas imports from Norway instead then UK-related national emissions could be higher than otherwise.

title: A CMO was horrified by how ChatGPT described her company. Here’s how she’s fixing it.
summary:
When Ameresco CMO Leila Dillon asked ChatGPT and other AI answer engines to describe what her company did, she was shocked by the results.
The publicly traded company is an energy infrastructure provider, helping power the rapidly growing AI buildout, as well as military bases and municipal facilities.
Dillon set about overhauling the company's messaging and how it structured its marketing content to better reflect its business.
Ameresco tracked how often AI chatbots mentioned the company in response to 50 questions that potential customers and investors might ask.
Those included:Updating its corporate boilerplate from "a leading cleantech integrator specializing in energy efficiency and renewable energy" to "a leading energy infrastructure company," reflecting the new positioning across its marketing and communications.

title: Will Jackdaw cut your energy bills?
summary:
The UK government has approved production from the Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea.
Ministers said the first gas could be produced by the end of this month, helping heat millions of homes, and also announced the creation of a new energy wealth fund.
BBC Verify correspondent Ben Chu looks at whether the approval of Jackdaw will mean lower bills for households and businesses.
